nameStory: Chinese bushclover gets its name from its native homeland in Asia, particularly China, where it naturally grows in grasslands and open areas. The 'bushclover' part describes its shrubby growth habit and its membership in the clover family, though it looks quite different from the familiar three-leaflet clovers we see in lawns. It's also called 'sericea lespedeza' - sericea means 'silky' in Latin, referring to the soft, silky hairs that cover its leaves and stems.
description: Chinese bushclover is a dense, upright perennial shrub that can grow 3-6 feet tall, forming thick colonies that crowd out native plants. It belongs to the legume family (the same family as peas and beans) and produces small clusters of creamy white to pale yellow flowers. The plant has a distinctive silvery-green appearance due to fine, silky hairs covering its narrow leaves and stems. Originally from Asia, it's now considered an invasive species in much of North America, including parts of New England.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Three narrow, wedge-shaped leaflets per leaf, each about 1/2 to 1 inch long, covered in soft, silvery hairs that give the whole plant a grayish-green appearance - run your finger along a leaf and feel the silky texture

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny creamy white to pale yellow pea-like flowers clustered tightly along the upper stems, each flower only about 1/4 inch long with the classic legume flower shape

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Dense, upright shrub that forms thick colonies, with multiple woody stems branching from the base - often so dense you can barely see through a patch

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Small, flat, oval seed pods about 1/8 inch long that don't split open, each containing a single seed and feeling papery when dry

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Slender, wiry stems covered in the same silky hairs as the leaves, becoming somewhat woody at the base with age

habitat: In New England, Chinese bushclover typically establishes in disturbed areas like roadsides, old fields, pastures, and forest edges, particularly in well-drained, sandy or clay soils. It thrives in full sun to partial shade and is often found along highway corridors and in abandoned agricultural areas. The plant tolerates poor soils and drought conditions, which helps it outcompete native vegetation in marginal habitats.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges as silvery-green shoots from the woody base, with the characteristic three-part leaves quickly becoming apparent.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming occurs from July through August, with dense clusters of small white to pale yellow flowers covering the upper portions of the stems.
seasonality.fall: Flowers develop into small, flat seed pods while leaves may turn yellowish before dropping, leaving behind the woody stem structure.
seasonality.winter: Dried stems and seed heads persist above ground, appearing as brown, brittle stalks that rattle in the wind when pods are present.

funFact: Chinese bushclover was intentionally planted across much of the United States in the mid-1900s for erosion control and wildlife food, but it turned out to be so aggressive that it can produce up to 2,000 seeds per plant and actually reduces wildlife habitat by forming dense monocultures that crowd out the diverse native plants that animals really need.
confusionNotes: Chinese bushclover is most easily confused with other bush clovers in the same genus, but its distinctive silvery, silky-hairy appearance sets it apart - if the plant looks like it's been dusted with silver, it's likely Chinese bushclover. Native bush clovers tend to be greener and less densely hairy, and usually don't form such thick, impenetrable colonies.
contextualKnowledge: Despite its common name including 'clover,' this plant is quite different from true clovers (Trifolium species) that we see in lawns - those have rounded leaflets and globe-shaped flower heads, while Chinese bushclover has narrow, wedge-shaped leaflets and small flowers in elongated clusters. As an invasive species, it's actively managed and removed in many conservation areas.
compareHints: Among New England's bush clovers, Chinese bushclover stands out for its silvery, densely hairy appearance and aggressive colonial growth habit. Native species like round-headed bush clover and violet bush clover are typically greener, less hairy, and grow as individual plants rather than forming dense thickets. Chinese bushclover also tends to be taller and more robust than most of its native relatives.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Round-headed bush clover stands out from its Lespedeza relatives by its distinctly round, compact flower heads - most other bush clovers have loose, elongated flower clusters or flowers scattered along the stems.
Among New England's bush clovers, hairy lespedeza stands out for its distinctly fuzzy, velvety texture covering the entire plant.
Among its bush clover relatives, violet bush clover stands out with its smooth (not hairy) stems and leaves, and its loose flower arrangement rather than dense round clusters.
Among New England's bush clovers, slender bush clover stands out for its delicate, wispy appearance with thin stems and small flower clusters.

Among its bush-clover relatives, tall bush-clover stands out with its reliably erect stems - round-headed bush clover has similar upright growth but denser, more rounded flower clusters, while violet bush clover and trailing lespedeza have more sprawling or leaning growth habits.
Among the many Lespedeza species, shrub lespedeza is unique in New England for its tall, shrubby growth habit - most other bush clovers in our region are low-growing or trailing plants.
Unlike its upright relatives like round-headed bush clover or hairy lespedeza that can reach several feet tall, trailing lespedeza never gets off the ground.
Among its bush clover relatives, narrow-leaved bush clover stands out for its distinctly slender leaflets and preference for wet soils.
Among the bush clovers in New England, violet bush clover stands out for its distinctly purple-violet flowers - most of its relatives have white, cream, or very pale pink blooms.
Among the lespedezas, Thunberg's is unique for its dramatic weeping form - most other bush clovers in New England grow upright or spreading but not with these long, graceful drooping branches.
While most of its lespedeza relatives like round-headed bush clover and violet bush clover grow upright in bushy clumps, creeping lespedeza is the ground-hugger of the family.
Downy lespedeza stands out from other bush clovers in New England primarily by its extremely fuzzy, silvery appearance.
